title: Lent: forty days
hook: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving, echoing Jesus in the desert

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash Wednesday, and your line: dust, and loved. Did you remember both halves when you washed your hands? The ash opens a season. Today, what comes next. Day one hundred fourteen.

Every spring you hear it at work, at school, in group chats. So what are you giving up for Lent? Chocolate. Coffee. Social media. Swearing. One person gives up nothing and says they're giving up giving things up. It can sound like a second round of New Year's resolutions. But the season started somewhere much older and much harder. In the Gospels, right after his baptism, Jesus goes out into the wilderness alone, and stays there. The King James says, "And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred." Hungry, alone, tested, in the desert. Today's word is the season Christians built around those forty days.
screen: `WHAT ARE YOU GIVING UP?` → `INTO THE WILDERNESS.` → `FORTY DAYS AND FORTY NIGHTS.`

segments.voice: Lent. It comes from an old English word for spring, when the days lengthen. In Greek and Latin the season is simply called the fortieth. Forty is a number the Bible keeps returning to. Forty days of rain for Noah. Forty days for Moses on the mountain. Forty years for Israel in the wilderness. Forty days for Elijah walking to the mountain of God. And forty days for Jesus in the desert. It's the Bible's number for a long, testing, transforming stretch. Lent is traditionally made of three practices, and they come from Jesus's own teaching in the Sermon on the Mount: prayer, fasting and giving to the poor. He doesn't say if you fast. He says when. Churches keep it differently. Catholics fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and many skip meat on the Fridays of Lent. Orthodox Christians keep the strictest fast, traditionally no meat, dairy or eggs for the whole of Great Lent. Many Protestants choose something personal, or take something up instead: reading a Gospel, volunteering, calling someone each day. Some churches don't mark Lent at all. But here's the idea that runs through all of them. Giving something up isn't meant as a punishment. It's meant to make room. The hour you'd spend scrolling becomes an hour for prayer. The money you'd spend on coffee goes to someone who needs it. The hunger itself becomes a reminder of what you're really hungry for. Less, so there's room. That's why Christians call it a season of preparation. It clears space for Easter.
screen: `LENCTEN: SPRING.` · `FORTY: THE BIBLE'S TESTING NUMBER.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, GIVING.` · `LESS, TO MAKE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one small Lenten thing. It doesn't have to be Lent right now. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself what's taking up too much room in your days. A habit, a screen, a snack, a complaint you keep repeating. Choose one small thing to set down for a week. Or choose one thing to take up in its place. Keep it small enough that you'll actually do it. If you pray, you can offer it to God. If you don't, just notice what fills the space. The bell holds the time.
Lent. From the old English for spring. Forty days of prayer, fasting and giving before Easter, echoing Jesus in the desert. Today's word.
Your line: less, so there's room. Today, start your small thing, and when you feel its absence, let the gap remind you what you made room for. Day one hundred fourteen.

what a scholar hears: English Lent from lencten, spring; Greek tessarakoste and Latin quadragesima, the fortieth. Western Lent counts forty days without the Sundays.

notes: Catholic discipline (fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday; abstinence from meat on Fridays of Lent) summarized; age limits omitted. Confirm.
Orthodox Great Lent fast (traditionally no meat, dairy, eggs; also fish, wine and oil on many days) simplified. Confirm.
Etymology: Old English lencten, spring (related to lengthening days). Confirm.
The forty examples: Noah (Gen 7:12), Moses (Ex 34:28), Israel (Num 14:33), Elijah (1 Kgs 19:8), Jesus (Matt 4:2). Confirm references.
Western reckoning: forty days not counting Sundays; Orthodox reckoning differs. Mentioned in the trapdoor only.
